title: Oil price shocks as IV for inflation on investment

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
We will use an instrumental variable (IV) approach to address the potential endogeneity of inflation with economic activity. The key assumption for this approach is the relevance and exogeneity of the instrument. In this case, we will use oil price shocks as an instrument for inflation. The relevance assumption requires that the instrument is correlated with the endogenous variable (inflation), and the exogeneity assumption requires that the instrument is uncorrelated with the error term in the structural equation (investment), conditional on the endogenous variable and other controls. The exclusion restriction assumption is that the instrument affects investment only through its effect on inflation, which is debatable in this case as oil prices may directly affect investment beyond the inflation channel.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(plm)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s24_data.csv")

# Convert the data to a panel data frame
pdata <- pdata.frame(data, index = c("id", "time"))

# First stage regression: inflation on oil price change
first_stage <- plm(x ~ z + controls, data = pdata, model = "within")

# Second stage regression: investment on predicted inflation
second_stage <- plm(y ~ x + controls, data = pdata, model = "within")

# Overidentification test (Hansen J test)
overid_test <- bptest(second_stage, ~x|1, vcov = vcovHC(second_stage, type = "HC1"))

# Print the results
summary(first_stage)
summary(second_stage)
overid_test

# Robustness check: using cluster-robust standard errors
vcov_cluster <- vcovHC(second_stage, type = "HC1", cluster = pdata$id)
coeftest(second_stage, vcov_cluster)
```

## 3. Expected Findings
We expect a negative coefficient on inflation in the second stage regression, indicating that higher inflation reduces corporate investment. The magnitude of the coefficient will depend on the strength of the relationship between inflation and investment. The sign and magnitude of the coefficient on the oil price change in the first stage regression will indicate the strength of the instrument. If the exclusion restriction holds, we expect the coefficient on the oil price change to be significant and positive in the first stage regression, indicating that oil price shocks are a valid instrument for inflation. However, if the exclusion restriction is violated, the coefficient on the oil price change may not be significant or may have the wrong sign, indicating that oil prices have a direct effect on investment beyond the inflation channel.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV/2SLS — oil price instrument; must defend exclusion restriction; test overidentification if multiple instruments
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Inflation reduces investment; exclusion restriction requires sector-level controls
